extracted.intended_audience: conference organizers, peer-review researchers, and practitioners building reviewer-paper matching algorithms
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation criteria for constructing a dataset of reviewer expertise and for comparing algorithms that compute reviewer-paper similarity (paper representations, reviewer profile choices, pooling methods, evaluation metrics, and statistical procedures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pooling methods for aggregating profile scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate similarity scores between a submitted paper and each paper in a reviewer's profile into a single similarity measure using pooling methods such as maximum, mean, or a percentile (e.g., 75th percentile).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common pooling methods: max and mean. Jhih-Yi et al. (2024) suggest using a percentile (such as the 75th percentile) to improve robustness against fraudulent behavior; the paper evaluates max, mean, and 75th-percentile pooling in Specter2 and reports that max pooling delivers the best performance while the 75th percentile performs nearly as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper representation choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a representation of paper content for similarity-computation algorithms from: (i) title only, (ii) title and abstract, (iii) full text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Option (ii) title+abstract is often used in real conferences and supported by most algorithms; richer representations (abstracts, full text) can improve accuracy but increase computational cost. Empirical findings: abstracts substantially improve over titles (~0.07 loss improvement) and full text provides additional (~0.03) improvement for TPMS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer profile construction (which papers to include)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide which papers to include in reviewers' profiles (e.g., the k most recent papers). In experiments, reviewer profiles were constructed using the 20 most recent papers from Semantic Scholar (include all if fewer than 20).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order papers by publication year and break ties uniformly at random. The choice of profile size affects information vs. relevance trade-offs: too few recent papers may miss information; too many older papers may add noise. Empirically, loss curves plateau once profiles include 8 or more most recent papers; practical recommendation: instruct reviewers to include ~10 representative papers (roughly 1-3 years of publications for active researchers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of full text when supported
rubrics_metrics.description: When algorithms can operate on full texts (e.g., TPMS), include full text to improve similarity estimation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TPMS benefits from full texts and can close the gap with embedding-based methods that cannot use full text. Full text yields additional improvement beyond title+abstract and is instrumental for improving performance on both easy and hard triplets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of baseline and interpreting performance deltas
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a simple baseline algorithm (TPMS chosen here) as a comparator; report ∆ = algorithm_loss − TPMS_loss (positive means worse than TPMS, negative means better).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TPMS was selected as a baseline for simplicity and because it can use full text. Present both absolute loss and 95% CI for loss, and 95% CI for ∆ to quantify relative performance; note that overlapping confidence intervals may limit decisive comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss metric that weights errors by expertise gap
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a loss metric that assigns smaller penalties to errors on pairs with similar reviewer expertise and larger penalties to errors on well-separated pairs (see Section 5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This loss aggregates performance into a single number but may obscure the types of mistakes; hence supplement with stratified evaluations (easy/hard triplets). Lower loss values are better. Construct 95% CIs (bootstrap) to quantify uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Easy versus hard stratification (triplet selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stratify evaluations by triplet difficulty: 'easy' triplets where a reviewer reported high expertise (≥4) on one paper and low expertise (≤2) on another; 'hard' triplets where the reviewer reported high expertise (≥4) on both papers but the expertise values differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Easy triplets test distinguishing high vs low expertise (important to avoid assigning irrelevant papers). Hard triplets test fine-grained distinctions among high-expertise papers (important to assign most suitable reviewers). Evaluate accuracy separately on these groups to understand algorithm strengths and weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy on triplet ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: For each triplet (reviewer r, papers p1, p2), compare the ordering predicted by an algorithm to the expertise-induced ordering and compute accuracy as the fraction of triplets correctly resolved (0–1, larger is better).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report accuracy with 95% confidence intervals for each algorithm and regime (title+abstract, full text, etc.). Use this alongside loss to characterize performance on easy and hard cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical evaluation procedures and uncertainty quantification
rubrics_metrics.description: Average out randomness in reviewer profile construction and quantify uncertainty in pointwise performance estimates using bootstrapping to create 95% confidence intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat profile construction and similarity prediction multiple times (10 in main experiments; 5 in some TPMS sweeps). To compute 95% CIs for loss, sample participants with replacement 1,000 times and recompute losses on the bootstrapped reviewer pool. For computational savings, reuse constructed profiles when profile-construction randomness is negligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper inclusion criteria for the dataset / survey
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey participants should report 5–10 papers in their broad research area that they read reasonably recently; reported papers should not be authored by the participant and should be freely available online (preferably arXiv).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestions to participants: choose some pairs that are well-separated and some that are close in expertise; avoid ties in ratings; include less famous or tricky examples to diversify the dataset; aim for at least 5 papers and up to 10.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise rating scale and meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect reviewer self-assessed expertise on a granular scale (example: 1.0 to 5.0 with intermediate steps: 1.0 = not qualified; 2.0 = can review some aspects but not reliably; 3.0 = adequate but substantial part outside expertise; 4.0 = background in most aspects with minor gaps; 5.0 = background necessary to evaluate all aspects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the scale to create triplets and compute loss/accuracy metrics; avoid ties when possible to produce richer training/evaluation signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove non-freely-available items from evaluations
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrict evaluations to papers whose PDFs are freely available; remove papers that are not freely available online from the dataset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures algorithms have access to the same information as human annotators and avoids missing data in representation-dependent methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling choice trade-offs and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly state and evaluate modeling choices that conference organizers face: paper representation (title/abstract/full text) and reviewer profile size, since these choices affect accuracy and computational cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report experiments varying these parameters (e.g., profile length 1–20 and three content regimes) and summarize findings (e.g., abstracts yield large gains over titles; full text helps further; performance plateaus after ~8 profile papers). Consider computation vs accuracy trade-offs when recommending production settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-transfer caution for pretrained algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious applying algorithms trained in one domain (e.g., ACL abstracts) to another domain (e.g., general ML) due to distribution shift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ACL algorithm was trained on computational-linguistics abstracts and may suffer distribution shift when applied outside that domain; nevertheless, it can be used without additional fine-tuning but results should be interpreted accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare to trivial baseline to verify usefulness of content
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a Trivial baseline to check that algorithms meaningfully leverage paper content (e.g., trivial baseline has much higher loss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All considered non-trivial algorithms substantially outperform the Trivial baseline in these experiments, confirming content is useful for expertise evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report and interpret confidence-interval overlap and dataset size limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: When confidence intervals for algorithm performance overlap, acknowledge that larger datasets are needed for finer-grained comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state limitations due to dataset size and sampling bias (e.g., uneven participant affiliations), and recommend continued data collection and replication with diverse methodologies.
